deep.reconstruction:
This page is a daily ephemeris for October. Rows 1–32 run from 1 October to 1 November, and row 32 is repeated as row 1 of the November page (p.143), just as row 31 of September repeats 1 October. Every column can be fitted to a closed formula (my identification, checked numerically against the entries). Write ☉ = λ for the Sun's true longitude, ε ≈ 23°28′ for the obliquity and k ≈ 20.6″ for an aberration-type constant. The table is the set of daily quantities needed to reduce fixed-star places for aberration and the solar part of nutation, essentially what Bessel later called the 'day numbers' A, B, C, D.

Col.1 (0.7515 … 0.8361): increases by exactly 0.00274 = 1/365.25 per day. It equals (N+0.5)/365.25, where N is the day of the year. Examples: 22 Sep, N=265, gives 0.7269; 1 Oct, N=274, gives 0.7515. So this is τ, the fraction of the year elapsed (the time argument of precession).

Col.5 (188°36′28″ … 219°20′21″): the Sun's true longitude λ. Daily increments are 58′58″ at the start of October and 59′57″ at the end, showing the speed-up toward perihelion.

Col.7 = C = −k cos ε cos λ. At λ=180° this gives 18.90 (table 18.91). At λ=188.61° it gives 18.69 (table 18.69). At λ=219.34° it gives 14.62 (table 14.62).

Col.6 = C·tan ε = −k sin ε cos λ. Check: col7/col6 is about 2.30 = cot ε throughout, e.g. 18.69·0.434 = 8.11. This is the 'C tan ε' combination that appears in the aberration of declination.

Col.8 = D = −k sin λ. It is zero at λ=180° (22 Sep). At 1 Nov it is 20.6·sin 39.34° = 13.06. At 30 Nov it is 20.6·sin 68.52° = 19.17 (table 19.18).

Col.9 and Col.10 put (C, D) into polar form for logarithmic computation. Col.9 is H with tan H = C/D, written as degrees.minutes. On 1 Oct, atan(18.69/3.08) = 80.64° = 80°38′. Col.10 is log10 h, with h = √(C²+D²). On 1 Oct, h = 18.94 and log h = 1.2775. On 1 Nov, h = 19.60 and log h = 1.2924. So the aberration in right ascension, C cos α + D sin α, becomes h sin(α + H).

Col.4 ≈ −0.43″ cos 2λ. It reads −0.43 at the equinox, crosses zero near λ = 225° (about 6–7 Nov) and reaches +0.32 by 30 Nov. This is B = −Δε for the solar (semi-annual) nutation in obliquity; modern Δε_sun = +0.57″ cos 2L.

Col.2 = A ≈ τ − 0.0196 sin 2λ. Col.2 equals col.1 at the equinox. The difference col.1 − col.2 is 0.0059 on 1 Oct, about 0.0195 at the start of November and 0.0136 at 30 Nov. That matches 0.0196 sin 2λ, which equals Δψ_sun/p with p ≈ 50.2″/yr annual precession and Δψ_sun ≈ −0.99″ sin 2λ (modern −1.32″).

The longitude amplitude divided by the obliquity amplitude is 0.99/0.43 ≈ 2.3, as theory requires. No lunar-nutation terms are visible: col.2 increments are smooth, with no fortnightly wiggles. So only the solar part seems to be tabulated here, the lunar 18.6-year part presumably being handled separately.

My fill-ins: all formula identifications and the constants k ≈ 20.6″, ε ≈ 23°28′, 0.43″ and 0.0196 are inferred by fitting. The manuscript itself carries no headings.
errors: No genuine computational errors found; spot checks of cols 6–10 against the inferred formulas agree to ±0.01″ or ±1′, consistent with rounding.
Col.9 entries agree to about 1′ when recomputed from the rounded C and D. For example, 1 Nov gives 48°14′ against the table's 48°13′, which is within rounding.
Several entries are overwritten corrections in the image: 3 Oct col.1, 5 Oct col.1, 25 Oct col.1 and 8 Oct col.7. All are consistent with the progression.

The aberration constant implied is about 20.6″, larger than Delambre's 20.25″ used around 1800. Either Gauss adopted a larger value or k absorbs another factor; this is not an error, but it is worth noting.

results.what: Daily tables of the aberration quantities C = −k cos ε cos☉, C tan ε and D = −k sin☉ for reducing star places
results.usually_credited_to: Bessel (Tabulae Regiomontanae, 1830), with earlier forms by Gauss, von Zach and others

results.what: Polar form h = √(C²+D²) and tan H = C/D, tabulated as log h and H, so that Δα·cosδ = h sin(α+H)
results.modern_name: Independent day numbers h, H (logarithmic form of the aberration reduction)

results.what: A ≈ τ + Δψ_sun/p and B = −Δε_sun, giving the solar semi-annual nutation (≈ −0.99″ sin2☉ in longitude, ≈ 0.43″ cos2☉ in obliquity)
results.modern_name: Besselian day numbers A, B (solar nutation part)
results.usually_credited_to: Solar nutation: Laplace / Lindenau around 1800–1810; day-number format: Bessel

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine computational ephemeris: daily aberration and solar-nutation reduction quantities for star places, in the day-number format. Gauss is known to have worked on and published aberration/nutation tables in von Zach's Monatliche Correspondenz around 1808, so such a table in his papers is unremarkable. It is mildly interesting as an early instance of the Bessel-style A, B, C, D and (h, H) scheme.
